title: Cassava bacterial blight
text: Cassava bacterial blight is caused by a bacterium that lives inside leaves and stems. Early signs are small, angular, water-soaked spots on the lower leaf surface that enlarge and turn brown, causing leaf blighting, wilting, and shoot tip die-back in severe cases. The petiole stays horizontal before leaves fall, unlike anthracnose-damaged leaves whose petioles droop. The bacterium spreads through infected stem cuttings, rain splash, contaminated tools, and insects such as grasshoppers, and damage is worse in the wet season and in young plants.

title: Cassava anthracnose disease
text: Cassava anthracnose disease is caused by a fungus that produces cankers, or sores, on stems and at the base of leaf petioles. The cankers weaken petioles so leaves droop and wilt, and soft stem parts can twist and break under severe attack, usually starting at the beginning of the rains. The fungus spreads by wind-borne spores from cankers and by planting infected stem cuttings, entering through wounds made by the bug Pseudotheraptus devastans. Besides cassava, the fungus also affects coffee, pepper, and pawpaw.

title: Cassava bud necrosis
text: Cassava bud necrosis is a fungal disease that appears as patches of brown or grey fungal growth covering the stem, sometimes over the buds, or eyes, of stem cuttings. Affected buds die, which reduces the sprouting ability of planting material taken from infected stems. The fungus survives on diseased cassava stems and debris left after harvest and spreads mainly through planting infected cuttings, so destroying diseased residues and selecting clean stems for planting material limits its spread.

title: Cassava leaf spot diseases
text: Three fungal leaf spot diseases occur on cassava: white leaf spot shows circular white or brownish-yellow spots often with purplish borders; brown leaf spot shows small brown spots with dark borders that can leave a shot-hole appearance as dead tissue falls out; and leaf blight shows larger light brown lesions not limited by leaf veins and lacking the water-soaked look of bacterial blight. All three spread from infected leaves on the plant or on the ground via wind or rain splash, and severe brown spot attack causes yellowing, drying, and early leaf death.

title: Cassava brown streak disease
text: Cassava brown streak disease is caused by a virus historically reported only in East and Southern Africa. Leaves show yellow patches mixed with normal green, more visible on mature leaves and without the leaf distortion seen in cassava mosaic disease. Stems develop dark brown streaks on the upper green portions and may show shoot tip die-back, while storage roots become distorted with cracks and brown discoloration. The virus spreads mainly through infected stem cuttings and is believed to also be transmitted by insects between plants.

title: Cassava root rot diseases
text: Cassava root rot is caused by various soil-living fungi that mainly occur in poorly drained soils and recently cleared forest fallow land. Affected plants show scorched, wilting, browning leaves, and both feeder and storage roots are killed; storage roots may swell unusually, develop light brown coloration inside, and give off a bad smell as they rot. The fungi spread through contaminated soil and infected root or stem debris, entering through wounds made by pests or farm tools, so cleaning tillage tools and burning infected plant debris helps limit spread. Root rot fungi also attack maize, soybean, sunflower, and coffee.

title: Why cassava diseases cause economic loss
text: Cassava diseases cause losses in several ways beyond direct root damage. Root rot and brown streak disease directly reduce storage root yield, while leaf and stem diseases interfere with the plant's ability to make and store food, reducing the number and size of storage roots even though most varieties tolerate some leaf loss without yield loss. Diseases that contaminate stems with viruses, bacteria, or fungi make cuttings unhealthy and unsuitable as planting material, and defoliation from disease encourages weed growth and, on loose soils, exposes soil to erosion.

title: When cassava diseases cause the worst losses
text: The timing of a cassava disease attack affects how much yield is lost. For example, under cassava mosaic disease, losses are higher when plants become infected within the first four months after planting than when infection happens later, and leaf spot diseases mainly occur on older leaves of plants over five to nine months old, making them unlikely to cause severe yield loss. Season also matters: bacterial blight and anthracnose damage is worse in the wet season, while brown streak symptoms are more serious in the dry season, and root rot can be severe in either season depending on the fungus involved.

title: Choosing healthy cassava planting material
text: Since most cassava diseases spread through infected stem cuttings, selecting healthy planting material is the main way to control them. Avoid stems showing leaf discoloration or chlorosis, leaf blighting and wilting, gum exudate, cankers, fungus patches, or streaks, since cuttings from such plants sprout into diseased seedlings or fail to sprout at all. For cassava mosaic disease specifically, take cuttings from branches rather than the main stem or basal portions where possible, and tag and select at harvest time the plants that sprouted without disease symptoms as future planting material.

title: Cassava variety tolerance to common diseases
text: Cassava varieties released across West and Central Africa differ in tolerance to major diseases and pests. For example, IITA variety TMS 30572 combines high yield potential with good tolerance to cassava green mite, cassava mosaic disease, and cassava bacterial blight, while Nigerian variety NR 8082 shows good tolerance across cassava green mite, mosaic disease, and bacterial blight along with high dry matter content. Selecting a variety with tolerance to the diseases common in a given locality, alongside good planting material and field sanitation, is a key part of integrated cassava disease management.

title: What Aflasafe is and how it controls aflatoxin
text: Aflasafe is a biological control product used in Nigeria to reduce aflatoxin contamination in maize and groundnut. It contains four naturally occurring, non-toxin-producing strains of the fungus Aspergillus flavus that were selected because they compete well and are widely adapted across Nigeria's growing regions. When applied to a field, these harmless strains outcompete the toxin-producing strains of the same fungus, so grain harvested from treated fields ends up carrying mostly the safe strains instead of the ones that cause dangerous aflatoxin levels.

title: How and when to apply Aflasafe in the field
text: Aflasafe is applied once per cropping season by uniformly broadcasting the coated sorghum-grain product by hand across the field at a rate of about ten kilograms per hectare, roughly two to three weeks before flowering. It should be applied to a normally managed, growing crop rather than after harvest, since the goal is for the beneficial fungus to establish in the field and be present on the crop before infection by toxin-producing strains can occur. Extension agents or trained field staff should supervise application to ensure even coverage and correct timing.

title: How much Aflasafe lowers aflatoxin at harvest
text: Across ten years of field trials and commercial use in Nigeria, maize and groundnut treated with Aflasafe consistently had far less aflatoxin at harvest than untreated crops from nearby fields, with reductions commonly in the range of seventy to ninety-five percent depending on the year and how much aflatoxin pressure untreated crops faced. In most years, treated maize and groundnut met the strict European Union limit of four micrograms per kilogram far more often than untreated crops, and almost none of the treated crop exceeded the United States action level of twenty micrograms per kilogram.

title: Aflasafe protection continues into storage
text: Aflasafe's benefit is not limited to the field: because the beneficial fungal strains become established on the crop before harvest, they continue to dominate over toxin producers if grain is stored under poor conditions that would otherwise favor fungal growth. In trials where maize and groundnut were deliberately subjected to simulated poor storage, aflatoxin levels in treated grain still rose far less than in untreated grain, with treated crops typically containing eighty to one hundred percent less aflatoxin than untreated crops after poor storage.

title: Aflasafe needs yearly application and reduces risk variation
text: Aflasafe should be applied every cropping season rather than a single time, similar to how certified seed or fertiliser is applied each season, because consistent yearly use gives the most reliable long-term protection. A further benefit of regular use is that it makes aflatoxin levels across a harvest much more consistent from sample to sample; grain lots from untreated fields show far more variation in contamination, meaning that even a lot testing low on average may still contain a few very unsafe samples, a risk that treated lots avoid.

title: How floods threaten food security in Nigeria
text: Flooding, especially in the Niger Delta, Lagos, and other coastal areas, damages Nigeria's mostly rain-fed agriculture by destroying crops, eroding topsoil, and wrecking irrigation infrastructure. The 2012 floods, among the worst in Nigerian history, displaced over two million people and drowned hundreds of hectares of farmland, sharply cutting output of staple crops like rice, maize, and cassava while destroying fisheries and livestock. Floods also damage roads and market access, causing post-harvest losses for farmers who cannot get produce to market and driving up food prices for low-income households.
origin: Akinkuolie, T.A., Ogunbode, T.O., Adekiya, A.O. (2025). Resilience to climate-induced food insecurity in Nigeria: a systematic review of the role of adaptation strategies in flood and drought mitigation. Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 8:1490133.

title: How droughts threaten food security in northern Nigeria
text: Droughts hit food security hardest in Nigeria's semi-arid northern regions, where farming depends mainly on rainfall. Extended dry spells deplete water for irrigation, lower soil moisture, and reduce yields of staple crops like millet, sorghum, and groundnuts that millions of Nigerians rely on. Droughts also cut livestock productivity and increase animal deaths from lack of water and poor pasture, which particularly harms pastoral communities in the north, and can intensify conflict between farmers and herders over scarce water and grazing land.

title: Zai pits for drought adaptation
text: Zai pits are small holes dug in a field before planting to collect and hold rainwater and organic matter around crops, and studies in northern Nigeria have shown they improve soil moisture retention and crop yields under drought-prone conditions. They are one of several traditional and low-cost water-harvesting techniques recommended for the semi-arid Sahel region of Nigeria, alongside drought-tolerant crop varieties and efficient irrigation such as solar-powered drip systems, to help smallholder farmers cope with erratic rainfall.

title: Community-based early warning for floods and droughts
text: Community-based early warning systems, where local climate information is gathered and shared at the community level, allow farmers to take timely action to protect crops and livelihoods ahead of floods or droughts. These systems work best when local communities are actively involved in designing and running them, since locally-tailored approaches address the specific vulnerabilities and capacities of each community rather than relying only on top-down national programmes.

title: Climate-smart agriculture practices for Nigerian farmers
text: Climate-smart agriculture combines practices that raise productivity, build resilience to climate shocks, and lower greenhouse gas emissions where possible. In Nigeria this includes conservation agriculture, which uses cover crops, crop rotation, and minimal soil disturbance to improve soil health, water retention, and yields; integrated soil fertility management, combining organic and inorganic fertilisers; and agroforestry, integrating trees and shrubs into farming systems to improve soil structure and biodiversity while adding resilience to climatic shocks.

title: Drought-tolerant maize varieties reduce risk in dry years
text: Drought-tolerant maize varieties developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture have been widely adopted in northern Nigeria and have been shown to yield more than standard varieties even in years with below-average rainfall. Adopting these varieties, particularly when combined with aligning planting dates to reliable rainfall onset, is highlighted as an important technological adaptation for reducing the risk of crop failure as drought frequency increases under climate change.

title: Why credit access limits climate adaptation for smallholders
text: A major barrier to smallholder farmers adopting climate-resilient technologies in Nigeria is limited access to credit: only around ten percent of smallholder farmers have access to formal credit, which restricts their ability to invest in tools such as solar-powered irrigation or drought-tolerant seed. Women farmers face additional barriers, since they often lack land ownership rights needed to secure credit, and limited access to agricultural extension services and climate information further slows the adoption of adaptive practices among both women and smallholders generally.

title: Matching climate adaptation strategies to Nigeria's regions
text: Because Nigeria's regions face different climate risks, adaptation strategies work best when tailored to local conditions. In the semi-arid Sahel region, drought-tolerant crop varieties, zai pits, and efficient irrigation are most relevant; in the flood-prone Niger Delta, flood-tolerant crops and community-based water management are the priority; and in the middle belt, a transition zone between arid and humid conditions, combined approaches such as conservation agriculture that address both drought and flood risk work best.

title: Aflatoxin risk differs by crop in the Sahel
text: A survey of maize, groundnut, and sorghum collected within one to two weeks of harvest across Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger found aflatoxin contamination in all three crops, but maize and groundnut were far more contaminated than sorghum. Average total aflatoxin levels reached hundreds of micrograms per kilogram in maize and groundnut in some regions, well above the European Union's four microgram per kilogram limit and the United States' twenty microgram per kilogram action level, showing that even freshly harvested grain can already carry unsafe aflatoxin levels from pre-harvest contamination.

title: Sorghum is less but not immune to aflatoxin risk
text: Sorghum is generally considered less susceptible to aflatoxin contamination than maize or groundnut, and this held true in the Sahel survey, where most sorghum samples had lower aflatoxin levels and a majority stayed under the strict European Union limit of four micrograms per kilogram. However, some sorghum samples still contained levels well above safe thresholds, particularly in Niger, showing that sorghum still needs aflatoxin management attention even though it is comparatively safer than maize and groundnut in the same growing region.

title: Why grain gets contaminated before harvest in the Sahel
text: Because samples were collected within one to two weeks of harvest, the high aflatoxin levels found indicate that contamination is occurring in the field before harvest, not just during storage, when fungal spores present in soil and crop debris infect the crop under favourable temperature and humidity conditions. Poor storage afterwards, including damp conditions and inadequate ventilation, can further raise aflatoxin levels, so integrated management addressing both pre-harvest field conditions and post-harvest drying and storage practices is needed to protect food safety.

title: Most African farms are small and low-input
text: A continental field survey across thousands of agricultural sampling locations in Africa found that most farms are small, with well over half of fields being less than about two hectares. External input use was also low: crop residues were retained on only about a quarter of fields, manure was applied on under a fifth of fields, and inorganic fertiliser was used on only about a fifth of fields, confirming a widespread pattern of nutrient mining and low-input smallholder agriculture across the continent.

title: Rainfed farming and weak soil and water conservation are widespread in Africa
text: The same continental soil survey found that ninety-four percent of sampled agricultural fields in Africa relied entirely on rainfall for water, with only about three percent irrigated, leaving most farms highly exposed to rainfall variability and climate shocks. Soil and water conservation measures such as vegetative barriers or structural works like bunds were absent on eighty-seven percent of fields, indicating that most African farmland lacks basic protection against erosion and water loss despite widespread vulnerability to land degradation.

title: Common physical soil constraints found across African farmland
text: Field surveyors across Africa commonly recorded physical soil constraints including compaction, coarse fragments in the soil, shallow effective rooting depth, and subsoil barriers that restrict root growth even in soils that appear deep at the surface. Woody vegetation cover on farmland was also found to be extremely sparse, which reduces organic matter inputs to soil, weakens soil structure, and raises erosion risk; roughly a fifth of surveyed agricultural land showed visible evidence of active soil erosion.

title: Cowpea aphid damage and control
text: Cowpea aphid (Aphis craccivora) attacks seedlings in large colonies on the underside of leaves and can also feed on green pods of older plants. Heavy sap-sucking causes wilting, distorted leaves and shoots, premature bud shedding, and shriveled flowers and pods, with severe infestations killing the plant. Damage is worse during dry spells when aphid populations build up quickly, and aphids also spread several plant viruses. Resistant varieties are the cheapest control; insecticides such as Imidacloprid, Pirimicarb, Dimethoate, or Lambda-cyhalothrin are used when infestation is heavy.

title: Cowpea thrips damage and control
text: Thrips (Megalurothrips sjostedti) feed on cowpea shoots and flower buds, causing distortion, drying, and shedding of flowers; they are also a vector of cowpea yellow mosaic virus. Populations are low during heavy rain but rise as the crop enters drier, later growth stages, and damage occurring before 42 days after planting rarely causes yield loss. Control options include intercropping cowpea with sorghum, millet, or cassava, planting resistant or early-maturing varieties, and insecticides such as cypermethrin or deltamethrin where infestation is severe.

title: Legume pod borer (Maruca) in cowpea
text: The legume pod borer (Maruca vitrata) is a regular cowpea pest whose larvae bore into flowers and green pods, and uncontrolled infestation can cause up to seventy percent yield loss. Young larvae feed inside flowers and cause flower drop, while older larvae are more mobile and feed at night, sheltering in flowers, pods, and leaf debris by day; webbing on flowers and pods is a visible sign of attack. Planting early or extra-early varieties can help the crop escape peak infestation, and insecticidal control with cypermethrin, lambda-cyhalothrin, or dimethoate is the most effective measure once Maruca is present.

title: Pod sucking bug complex in cowpea
text: A complex of pod sucking bugs, including Clavigralla tomentosicollis and related species, causes serious cowpea yield loss when populations are large. Both nymphs and adults suck sap from green pods, causing seed-coat dimpling, pod abortion or shedding, premature drying, and deformed, poorly filled seeds. Planting early or extra-early varieties helps the crop escape peak infestation, and a mixture of dimethoate and cypermethrin is the most effective insecticidal control once the pest is established.

title: Timing insecticide sprays for cowpea insect pests
text: Cowpea spray timing is built around the crop's growth stages: a first spray thirty to thirty-five days after planting targets early thrips, aphids, and Maruca at bud initiation; a second spray at forty to forty-five days covers full bloom and early podding against thrips and Maruca; a third spray at fifty to sixty days protects the rapid pod-filling stage against Maruca and pod sucking bugs; and a fourth spray, if needed, at sixty-five to seventy-five days addresses heavy pod-sucking-bug pressure on medium-maturing varieties. Improved varieties typically need two to three sprays per season while local varieties may need up to four, and a single spray is most effective if applied at budding or flowering.

title: Maize stem borer damage and control
text: Maize stem borer (Busseola fusca) is the most important maize pest in Nigeria's dry savanna, with larvae feeding on leaves and tunneling into young plants, sometimes killing the central leaves in a 'dead heart' pattern. In mature plants larvae bore into the main stem and later into tassels and cobs, and just one to two larvae per plant can cut yield by up to twenty-five percent. Control relies mainly on removing and burning damaged stems and cobs from the field and plowing in crop residues to kill larvae, since chemical control at this stage is difficult and costly.

title: Maize leaf hopper and streak virus
text: Leaf hopper (Cicadulina mbila) pierces maize tissue to feed on sap and is the vector of maize streak virus; heavy feeding can wither the plant, and populations peak late in the growing season, making late-sown maize especially vulnerable. Recommended control is to plant early, burn infected plants promptly to remove virus sources, and spray carbaryl to reduce hopper numbers where infestation is heavy.

title: Termite damage in maize fields
text: Termites attack maize roots and lower stems, building nests at the plant base, with damage worse under heavy water stress and more common on established plants than seedlings. Feeding weakens the plant, leading to lodging and, through damage to vascular tissue, wilting under water stress. Control focuses on avoiding continuous cultivation of the same land, practicing crop rotation, avoiding heaps of crop residue or manure that attract termites, and treating seed with insecticide, since chemical control of established colonies is difficult and should be a last resort.

title: Safe pesticide spraying practices
text: Safe pesticide spraying requires long-sleeved clothing, trousers, covered shoes, and eye protection, plus the correct nozzle type and flow rate for the target pest and chemical. Farmers should never spray against or across the wind, never spray in very windy or completely still conditions, never walk directly into a freshly sprayed field, and never smoke, eat, or drink during spraying. Unused crop protection product should never be left in an open container, and only reputable, properly labeled products should be purchased and used strictly according to label instructions.

title: First aid for pesticide poisoning
text: If pesticide poisoning is suspected, first move the affected person away from the contamination to a recovery position, then read the product label for specific first aid guidance. Wash the eyes and skin with available water, remove contaminated clothing, and give artificial respiration if breathing is poor; do not induce vomiting unless the label specifically recommends it. Medical attention should be sought immediately in every suspected poisoning case, staying calm throughout so the response is not delayed.

title: Dry-season stover and fodder feeding rates
text: During the dry season, sheep and goats should be offered about one kilogram per animal per day of chopped cereal stover plus two hundred to three hundred grams of legume fodder, supplemented with grain byproducts such as wheat, maize, millet, sorghum, or soybean bran when affordable. Cattle need about two to three percent of body weight per day, fed as a cereal-legume mixture in a two-to-one ratio and supplemented with grain byproducts where available. Confining animals to feed stored residues at the onset of the dry season, rather than relying on free grazing, helps maintain live weight through the feed-scarce period.

title: Benefits of integrating crops and livestock
text: Integrating crop and livestock production lets legume and cereal residues be converted into animal feed while manure returns fertility to the farmland, reducing dependence on inorganic fertiliser and helping control erosion. Confined, better-fed animals are easier to monitor for health, show improved fertility, and are more secure from theft or loss than free-grazing stock. The approach also diversifies farm income across grain, fodder, meat, and milk, and generates rural employment that can reduce youth migration away from farming areas.

title: PICS triple-bagging for cowpea storage
text: The Purdue Improved Cowpea Storage (PICS) method uses three nested polyethylene bags, each about eighty microns thick, to create an airtight seal that starves storage bruchids of oxygen without any chemicals. Cowpea must be thoroughly sun-dried and cooled before filling the innermost bag nearly to capacity, rocking the bags to remove air pockets, then tightly tying off each of the three bags in sequence. Sealed bags should stay closed for at least two months, and once opened, the required quantity should be removed quickly and the bag re-sealed promptly to prevent bruchids from re-infesting the grain.

title: Mineral and oil protectants for stored cowpea
text: Where hermetic bags are unavailable, cowpea in storage can be protected from bruchids using low-cost minerals: one kilogram of fine sand mixed with ten kilograms of cowpea seed, or one kilogram of wood ash mixed with forty kilograms of seed. Vegetable oils also provide roughly three months of protection, applied at five millilitres of groundnut oil or three millilitres of neem seed oil per kilogram of cowpea seed. These low-cost, non-chemical methods are useful where hermetic storage bags are not accessible to farmers.

title: Recognizing and preventing mold in stored grain
text: Mold in stored cowpea and cereal grain is harder to spot than insect or rodent damage, but it breaks down grain tissue, causes bad taste and odor, reduces seed germination, and can produce mycotoxins that harm the liver, kidney, brain, or skin of people and animals who eat contaminated grain. Mold thrives in warm, humid conditions, so proper sun-drying before storage is the single best prevention, along with keeping stored grain dry, well-ventilated, and off damp surfaces. Regularly inspecting sacks by hand and looking for discoloration, texture change, or fungal growth helps catch mold problems early.

title: Rodent management in grain stores
text: Rodents damage stored grain by eating it directly, contaminating it with droppings, and gnawing holes in storage sacks, while also carrying diseases harmful to people. Management combines trapping, rodenticides such as fast-acting zinc phosphide bait or slower-acting anticoagulants like warfarin, and biological or physical control such as keeping cats and sealing structural gaps that let rodents enter. Every storage facility should be checked for cracks and holes before use and repaired promptly, since access points are the main way rodents reach stored grain.

title: Manure and NPK basal dose for cowpea
text: Cowpea fixes its own nitrogen through a symbiotic relationship with soil rhizobium bacteria, so it performs well even under low-nitrogen conditions and rarely needs seed inoculation in Nigeria, where the bacteria are already widespread. A starter rate of about fifteen kilograms of nitrogen per hectare can help early growth on very poor soils, but excess nitrogen promotes excess leafy growth, delays maturity, and can suppress the plant's own nitrogen fixation. The recommended base fertility program is at least one tonne per hectare of animal manure plus one hundred kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 (or single super phosphate), broadcast and worked into the soil before planting.

title: Cowpea spacing and seed rate
text: Recommended cowpea spacing for improved varieties is seventy-five centimetres between rows and twenty centimetres within rows, narrowing to fifty centimetres between rows for early and extra-early maturing types. Three seeds are sown per hill and thinned to two plants per hill about two weeks after sowing, though thinning is optional if labour cost is a concern. About twenty to twenty-five kilograms of seed is needed to plant one hectare as a sole crop, and cowpea should only be planted after a good rain of fifteen millimetres or more, since dry planting risks poor germination.
